title: A poor childhood
hookLine: his father died young, and as a boy he worked in a hospital for the poor in Medina del Campo

cards: A young man from a comfortable family falls in love with a poor girl who weaves silk for a living. His family says: marry her, and you're out. He marries her anyway, and they're cut off.
They have three sons. They're poor, but they're together. Then, when the youngest is still a toddler, the father gets sick and dies.
The mother walks for miles with her small children to ask the rich relatives for help. They mostly turn her away. The toddler grows up to be John of the Cross.

teach.b: First, hunger. John was born Juan de Yepes in 1542, in a small Castilian town called Fontiveros. His father, Gonzalo, died when John was very small.

His mother, Catalina, kept the family alive by weaving, moving from town to town looking for work. It wasn't enough. One of John's brothers, Luis, died young, and some biographers think hunger was part of it.
The family finally settled in Medina del Campo, a busy market town, and John was taken into a school for poor and orphaned children, where he got food, clothes and some learning.
They tried to apprentice him to a trade: carpenter, tailor, woodcarver, painter. None of them stuck. Third, the hospital.

teach.h: WASHING THE SICK AS A TEENAGER.
teach.b: As a teenager he worked in a hospital for the poor, a place for people with contagious diseases. He washed patients, fed them, cleaned up after them, and went out begging in the streets to pay for their care.
People who knew him then remembered how gentle he was with the sick. Fourth, the choice. The hospital's director saw something in him and paid for him to study with the Jesuits.

teach.h: HE TURNS DOWN A SAFE FUTURE.
teach.b: He offered John a secure future: become a priest and stay on as the hospital's chaplain. For a poor boy, that was everything. John said no, and quietly joined the Carmelites at twenty-one.
The man who later wrote about nights and nothingness wasn't theorizing.
He knew poverty, hunger and sickrooms first.

how: Catholics remember John of the Cross's early years of poverty and hospital work, and visiting the sick is one of the corporal works of mercy in Catholic teaching.

o: the want that marked John's poor, fatherless childhood
a famine that struck all of Spain when John was born
a tax his family had to pay the king each year

games.q: who was the boy — tap the pairs.
p: his father, cut off for love
the market town where he grew up
where he washed and fed the sick

s: John of the Cross came from a comfortable family
his father was cut off for marrying a poor weaver, then died young. John grew up poor and hungry.
as a teenager he begged in the streets for a hospital
he nursed the sick poor and collected alms for their care.
he tried several trades before finding his way
carpenter, tailor, woodcarver, painter. none of them stuck.

games.q: you're John, twenty-one, a poor boy. the hospital director offers to make you a priest and the hospital's chaplain, a safe life for good. what do you do?
o: accept; you'll never be hungry again.
turn it down and quietly join the Carmelites.
leave for the university and a career.
games.why: he said no to the safe future and joined the Carmelites in 1563. it wasn't the easy road, and it wouldn't get easier.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's sick right now, in body or in spirit: a friend in the hospital, a parent getting frail, a coworker who's been quietly struggling.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, send them good attention. Then choose one small, concrete thing you could do for them: a text, a meal, a visit, a ride.

wordCard.voice: Hunger. What marked John of the Cross's childhood: a father's early death, a mother who wove for pennies, and a brother hunger may have taken too. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: he knew poverty first. Before the poems came the sickrooms. See you tomorrow.
